tip: On its own this letter keeps its short /a/ sound, as in 'cat'. The tricky part: in a sentence we say it quickly and softly, like 'uh' — 'a cat' sounds like 'uh cat'.
The 's' at the end says /z/, not its usual hissy sound — listen for 'iz'.
You'll spot 'the' everywhere in a story — the tricky bit is the ending, which says a quick 'thuh' instead of the 'eh' sound e usually makes.
In 'to' the o makes a long 'oo' sound instead of its short sound — think of it as a tiny pointing word, always heading off to somewhere.
Sound out p-u-t. The tricky part is the u: in 'put' it says a short /oo/, as in 'book' (in many accents). Say it the way your class says it.
'I' is only one letter but it's always written tall as a capital, and it says its own name rather than the short i sound, because it means me — the person talking.
You've only learned the short o so far, like in 'dog', but in 'no' the o says its long name 'oh' instead — two letters for one big, definite word.
Just like 'is', the 's' at the end says /z/ — it rhymes with 'fizz', not with 'hiss'.
The 's' at the end says /z/ again — is, his and has all share this same trick, so learn them as a family.
Just like 'no', the o in 'go' says its long name 'oh' rather than the short sound from 'dog' — picture the two letters setting off on a journey.
The 'f' here says /v/, not its usual sound — say it out loud and you'll hear 'ov', not 'off'.
Sound out a-s. The tricky part is the s at the end: it says /z/, so 'as' sounds like 'az' — the same trick as is, his and has.
Once you know 'in' and 'to', you already know 'into' — just listen for the o at the end saying 'oo', not its short sound.

A name. Sound out O-l-i-v. The tricky part is the e at the end: it makes no sound. It is there because English words hardly ever end in v. In Year 1, children learn 've' as a spelling and can read Olive's name with no tricky part.
